subject: Copywriting
title: Gary Vaynerchuk: Jab Jab Jab Right Hook
description: A fast breakdown of Gary Vaynerchuk: Jab Jab Jab Right Hook for builders.

hook.text: Gary Vee turned a wine shop into a $60M business with YouTube videos. Then he wrote the playbook for social copy.

buildup.text: His 'Jab Jab Jab Right Hook' framework: give value three times before you ask for anything. Earn the right to sell.

discovery.text: He analyzed hundreds of social media posts and showed why most brand copy fails: too many asks, not enough giving.

twist.text: Critics call him loud and shallow. But his framework is Cialdini's reciprocity repackaged for the social media age.

climax.text: Whether you love or hate him, his JJJRH model is used by every social media manager crafting content calendars.

punchline.text: Give, give, give, then ask. Social copy in four beats.

quiz.question: What does 'Jab Jab Jab Right Hook' mean in copywriting?
options: Give value three times before asking for something

details.summary: Gary Vaynerchuk popularized the idea that brands must give value repeatedly ('jabs') before asking for a sale ('right hook'). His framework, outlined in 'Jab, Jab, Jab, Right Hook,' argues that social media copy must be native to each platform and prioritize community over conversion.
details.whyItMatters: Vaynerchuk reshaped how brands think about social media copywriting. His value-first approach anticipated the shift from interruptive advertising to permission-based content creation.
takeaways: Give value (jabs) three times before making a sales ask (right hook)
Copy must be native to each social platform's culture and format
Building community precedes driving conversions in social media

faq.question: What does 'jab, jab, jab, right hook' mean?
faq.answer: Jabs are pieces of content that give value — entertainment, education, or inspiration — without asking for anything. The right hook is the sales ask. Vaynerchuk's rule is that you must earn the audience's attention and trust through jabs before you have the right to sell.

faq.question: Why does Vaynerchuk emphasize platform-native content?
faq.answer: Each social platform has its own culture, format, and audience expectations. Copy that works on LinkedIn fails on TikTok. Vaynerchuk argues that repurposing identical content across platforms is lazy and ineffective — great social copy respects the platform it appears on.
